items.title: Public market equivalent (PME)
items.text: The Kaplan-Schoar PME divides a fund's distributions, discounted at the S&P 500 total return, by its capital calls discounted the same way, all net of fees. Above 1.0 means the fund beat the index on a cash-flow-matched basis.

items.title: DPI and TVPI
items.text: DPI (distributions to paid-in capital) counts only value returned to LPs in cash through exits or other liquidity events. TVPI (total value to paid-in) adds unrealized holdings at their current marks. A fund can show strong TVPI with near-zero DPI.

items.text: A deterministic cash-flow model for illiquid funds: capital calls are a time-varying fraction of uncalled commitments, distributions a time-varying fraction of the fund's asset value, and returns are constant. Later work, such as Luxenberg et al. (2022), builds on it to model calls, distributions and asset value.

items.title: The Arithmetic of Active Management
items.text: Because passive investors hold the market and earn its return, active investors as a group must also earn the market return before costs. After their higher costs, the average actively managed dollar must therefore trail the average passively managed dollar. Contrary evidence reflects measurement errors.

items.title: The Performance of Mutual Funds in the Period 1945-1964
items.text: Introduced Jensen's alpha, a CAPM-based measure of risk-adjusted performance. Across 115 funds from 1945 to 1964, funds on average could not beat a buy-and-hold strategy, even measured before management expenses, and few individual funds did better than chance would predict.

items.title: On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance
items.text: Using survivor-bias-free data, common factors in stock returns, including one-year momentum, plus fund expenses almost fully explain persistence in mutual fund returns. The only strong unexplained persistence is the underperformance of the worst funds, and the results do not support the existence of skilled or informed managers.

items.title: Mutual Fund Flows and Performance in Rational Markets
items.text: A rational model in which skilled managers face decreasing returns to scale. Investors chase past performance, flows grow funds until expected excess returns vanish, so performance does not persist and average funds do not beat passive benchmarks, even though managers have real and varied skill.

items.title: Relative Strength Index (RSI)
items.text: Wilder's RSI is a 0 to 100 momentum oscillator: RSI = 100 - 100/(1 + RS), where RS is average gain over average loss, by default over 14 periods with Wilder smoothing. Wilder treated readings above 70 as overbought and below 30 as oversold.

items.title: Average True Range (ATR)
items.text: True range is the largest of: today's high minus low, high minus prior close, or low minus prior close (absolute values). ATR, from Wilder (1978), averages true range over 14 periods, then smooths it as (prior ATR x 13 + current TR) / 14. It measures volatility, not direction, and is used for stop and position sizing.

items.title: Average Directional Index (ADX)
items.text: Wilder's directional movement system uses +DI and -DI (smoothed directional movement divided by smoothed true range) for direction, and ADX, a smoothed average of their normalized difference, for trend strength. Default is 14 periods. Wilder saw ADX above 25 as a strong trend and below 20 as no trend.

items.title: Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD)
items.text: MACD, invented by Gerald Appel in the late 1970s, is the 12-day EMA minus the 26-day EMA of closing prices. The signal line is a 9-day EMA of MACD, and the histogram is MACD minus signal. It turns two trend-following averages into a momentum oscillator.

items.text: John Bollinger's bands are a moving average (default 20 periods) with upper and lower bands a multiple (default 2) of the population standard deviation away. They show whether price is high or low relative to recent volatility. Companion measures are %b (position within the bands) and BandWidth (band width relative to the middle band).

Derives an efficient frontier of execution schedules under linear temporary and permanent impact, shows an even-slice schedule is never optimal for a risk-averse trader, and defines liquidity-adjusted VaR.

items.title: Anomalous Price Impact and the Critical Nature of Liquidity in Financial Markets
items.text: Proposes a theory in which the average supply and demand profile is V-shaped and nearly vanishes at the current price. This forces large orders to be split, explaining long memory in order signs, and makes price impact grow roughly with the square root of order size rather than linearly: the square-root impact law.

items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: arXiv: six authors, May 2011, Physical Review X 1, 021006 (2011); abstract: V-shaped profile vanishing at price, metaorder splitting, long memory, square-root impact.

items.title: Price Impact
items.text: A review of how price impact is measured and modeled. Signed order flow and price changes are strongly linked, but the impact of trades is neither linear in volume nor permanent. Impact is how private information enters prices, and random order-flow fluctuations also add to volatility.

items.title: On the Impossibility of Informationally Efficient Markets
items.text: If gathering information is costly, prices cannot fully reflect it, or no one would be paid to gather it. Equilibrium needs an 'equilibrium degree of disequilibrium' where prices are partly informative and informed traders earn a return on research. Noise is needed for trade; perfectly efficient markets would be thin.
items.source_title: American Economic Review 70(3): 393-408
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: AEA PDF: AER 70(3) 393-408, June 1980; 'equilibrium degree of disequilibrium' present; noise needed; informative markets very thin.

items.title: Noise
items.text: Argues that noise, in the sense of a large number of small events, makes trading in financial markets possible and lets us observe prices. It also makes markets somewhat inefficient while often stopping anyone from exploiting the inefficiency, and makes theories about markets very hard to test.
items.source_title: The Journal of Finance 41(3): 528-543
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref: Black, JF 41(3) 528-543, July 1986; abstract: noise makes trading possible, somewhat inefficient, hard to test theories.

items.title: Noise Trader Risk in Financial Markets
items.text: Models irrational noise traders whose unpredictable beliefs move prices. Because those beliefs are unpredictable, rational arbitrageurs face risk and cannot bet aggressively against them, so prices can stay far from fundamentals and noise traders can even earn higher expected returns. Helps explain excess volatility and closed-end fund discounts.
items.source_title: Journal of Political Economy 98: 703-738

items.title: The Limits of Arbitrage
items.text: Real-world arbitrage takes capital and carries risk, and is done by a small number of specialists using other people's money. As a result arbitrage can fail in extreme situations, when prices move far from fundamentals, and the model predicts where anomalies are likely to persist.

items.title: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk
items.text: Shows that people's choices under risk violate expected utility. People value gains and losses relative to a reference point, with a value function concave for gains, convex for losses and steeper for losses (loss aversion). They underweight probable outcomes versus certain ones and overweight small probabilities.

items.title: Taleb (2019), How much data do you need? A pre-asymptotic metric for fat-tailedness
items.text: Proposes kappa, a measure scaled from 0 (Gaussian, thinnest) to 1 (maximally fat-tailed), based on how fast the law of large numbers works for sums of n terms. Meant to tell how many observations are needed and to compare distribution classes where kurtosis or tail index fail. International Journal of Forecasting 35(2), 677-686, April 2019.
items.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? An Operational, Pre-Asymptotic Metric for Fat-tailedness (arXiv 1802.05495; DOI 10.1016/j.ijforecast.2018.10.003)
items.publisher: International Journal of Forecasting (Elsevier); preprint on arXiv
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: arXiv abstract matches; Crossref: IJF 35(2) 677-686, April 2019, sole author Taleb.

items.title: Taleb's kappa: formula
items.text: With S_n the sum of n i.i.d. draws and M(n) = E|S_n - E(S_n)| (mean absolute deviation of the sum), kappa(n0, n) = 2 - [log(n) - log(n0)] / log[M(n)/M(n0)]. Equivalently M(n)/M(n0) = (n/n0)^(1/(2-kappa)). Shorthand kappa_n0 uses n = n0 + 1; kappa_1 compares one draw with two.
items.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? (arXiv 1802.05495v3, Definition 1 and Eq. 1)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Eq. 1 and M(n)/M(n0)=(n/n0)^(1/(2-kappa)) match; kappa_n0 = kappa(n0, n0+1).

items.title: Kappa for the Gaussian is 0
items.text: The paper states kappa equals 0 for the Gaussian: the mean absolute deviation of a sum grows with the square root of n, the fastest convergence. For stable laws with tail exponent alpha at least 1, kappa = 2 - alpha.
items.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? (arXiv 1802.05495v3)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Paper: kappa=0 for Gaussian; kappa=2-alpha for stable with alpha>=1.

items.title: Kappa for the Cauchy is 1
items.text: From the paper's stable-law relation kappa = 2 - alpha, the Cauchy (stable alpha = 1) has kappa = 1, the maximum: averaging more Cauchy draws does not shrink dispersion at all, so no sample is large enough. The paper also notes a high-sigma lognormal behaves like a one-tailed Cauchy, kappa near 1.
items.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? (arXiv 1802.05495v3)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Cauchy value is derived from kappa=2-alpha as the item says (paper gives no explicit Cauchy row); lognormal high-sigma 'one-tailed Cauchy', kappa near 1 confirmed.

items.title: Kappa for Student T with alpha 3 (a common fit for equity returns)
items.text: Table II gives Student T alpha = 3: kappa_1 = 0.29, kappa_1,30 = 0.191, kappa_1,100 = 0.159. Pareto alpha = 3 is fatter: 0.465, 0.3246, 0.281. The exponential has kappa_1 of about 0.21. Values between 0 and 1 rank how much extra data a distribution needs relative to a Gaussian.
items.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? (arXiv 1802.05495v3, Tables I and II)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Table II: Student alpha=3 0.29/0.191/0.159; Pareto 0.465/0.3246/0.281; exponential kappa_1 ~ .21 in Table I.

items.title: Taleb and Douady (2013), Mathematical definition, mapping, and detection of (anti)fragility
items.text: Defines fragility and antifragility as negative or positive sensitivity to a semi-measure of dispersion and volatility (a 'vega'), model-free and applicable to any payoff with a distribution. Proposes a simple detection heuristic said to reveal hidden risks from size, forecasting and bank tail exposures. Quantitative Finance 13(11), 1677-1689, November 2013.
items.source_title: Mathematical Definition, Mapping, and Detection of (Anti)Fragility (arXiv 1208.1189; DOI 10.1080/14697688.2013.800219)
items.publisher: Quantitative Finance (Taylor and Francis); preprint on arXiv
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: arXiv abstract matches (vega, model-free heuristic, size/forecasting/bank hidden risks); Crossref: Quant Finance 13(11) 1677-1689, Nov 2013.

items.title: Fragility in one sentence (Taleb-Douady)
items.text: Fragility is the sensitivity of the left-tail shortfall below a threshold K (the integral of (x - Omega) f(x) from minus infinity to K, not conditioned on probability) to a change in the left semi-deviation of the distribution; an engine can estimate it by bumping volatility and measuring how much expected tail loss grows.
items.source_title: Mathematical Definition, Mapping, and Detection of (Anti)Fragility (arXiv 1208.1189v1)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: PDF defines fragility as sensitivity of unconditional left-tail shortfall xi(K,s-) = integral (x-Omega) f(x) to left semi-deviation.

items.title: Taleb-Douady detection heuristic
items.text: Their heuristic measures how a valuation or payoff responds to finite shifts of each parameter up and down by a step delta, and compares the two changes as a second-order (convexity) test: losses that accelerate with larger shocks signal fragility. The paper claims this beats stress testing and Value-at-Risk at revealing hidden tail exposure.
items.source_title: Mathematical Definition, Mapping, and Detection of (Anti)Fragility (arXiv 1208.1189)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: PDF heuristic: finite shifts Delta p, second-order ratio H vs 1; abstract says it outperforms stress testing and VaR.

items.title: Taleb on ruin and ergodicity
items.text: Taleb separates ensemble probability (outcomes across many people at once) from time probability (one person repeating a bet). With any chance of ruin these diverge: a repeated bet with ruin risk reaches eventual bust with 100% probability, so average-of-population returns do not apply to the individual and cost-benefit analysis breaks down. Survival comes first.

items.title: Split conformal coverage guarantee
items.text: With n calibration points exchangeable with the test point, split conformal sets satisfy 1 - alpha <= P(Y_test in C(X_test)) <= 1 - alpha + 1/(n+1). The threshold is the empirical quantile of calibration scores at level ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n. The guarantee is marginal (on average over points), not conditional on today's regime.

Under drift, coverage can fall below 1 - alpha by an amount tied to distribution shift, so empirical coverage must be monitored in walk-forward tests.

items.text: A label is set by whichever barrier the price path hits first: an upper profit-taking barrier (label 1), a lower stop-loss barrier (label -1), or a vertical time barrier ending the trade. items.title: Pearl: proof of work by matrix multiplication
items.text: Pearl is a Bitcoin-style Layer 1 that "replaces SHA-256 hashing with matrix multiplication as its proof of work function." "The chain has a fixed 2.1B PRL supply and targets 194-second blocks." Miners commit to their input matrices first, and the result is verifiable by other nodes without re-running the full workload.

items.title: Pearl's duplex work: the same matmuls earn twice
items.text: "That work is matrix multiplications, the core math behind AI inference (running a trained model to answer requests)." "AI revenue helps pay for the machines; PRL rewards become extra income." Bankless describes Pearl as a fork of Bitcoin that launched in April, with launch inference prices up to roughly 75% below a major provider's standard rates, potentially subsidized by mining rewards.

items.title: Pearl's issuance front-loads supply
items.text: Pearl's issuance "follows a smooth, polynomial decay curve rather than Bitcoin's four-year halvings." "About half its supply is mined in the first four years", so inflation falls each year, to roughly 30% by year three and about 11% by year five.
